```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(simling)
```

## The data {.smaller}

In `n400`, 30 participants read German sentences that end in an expected or an unexpected word (*Er trinkt seinen Kaffee / Schrank*) while their EEG is recorded. `amplitude` is the mean EEG signal in microvolts (µV), 300 to 500 ms after the last word. Unexpected words make it more negative: this is the [N400]{.hl}. Each participant reads 80 items, 40 in each condition. Today we use only the electrode Cz, at the top of the head:

```{r}
cz <- n400 |>
  filter(electrode == "Cz")
glimpse(cz)
```

Today's question: how large is the N400 effect, and how sure can we be about it?

---

## 1. Fitting the model

### 1.1 Condition means

Compute the mean `amplitude` in each `condition`. How large is the difference?

::: solution

```{r}
cz |>
  summarise(amplitude = mean(amplitude), .by = condition)
```

:::

### 1.2 Which random effects?

Each participant reads items in both conditions, and each item has an expected and an unexpected version. Fit this model and save it as `m`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
m <- lmer(amplitude ~ condition + (1 + condition | participant) + (1 | item), data = cz)
```

Why does the model have a varying slope for `condition` by participant? Look at the fixed effects with `fixef(m)`. What do the intercept and the slope mean?

::: solution

```{r}
m <- lmer(amplitude ~ condition + (1 + condition | participant) + (1 | item), data = cz)
fixef(m)
```

The condition changes within each participant, and participants may differ in how strong an N400 they show, so their slopes can vary.

The intercept, `r round(fixef(m)[1], 2)` µV, is the mean amplitude after an expected word. After an unexpected word, the amplitude is `r round(abs(fixef(m)[2]), 2)` µV more negative: the N400 effect.

:::

### 1.3 The truth

In the true model behind the data (`?n400`), the N400 at Cz is −4 µV times (1 − cloze), where cloze is how predictable a word is. Use the mean `cloze` of each condition to compute the true difference between the conditions. Is the estimate close?

::: solution

```{r}
cz |>
  summarise(cloze = mean(cloze), .by = condition)
cloze_expected <- mean(cz$cloze[cz$condition == "expected"])
cloze_unexpected <- mean(cz$cloze[cz$condition == "unexpected"])
-4 * (1 - cloze_unexpected) - -4 * (1 - cloze_expected)
```

The true difference is about `r round(-4 * (cloze_expected - cloze_unexpected), 1)` µV, and the estimate, `r round(fixef(m)[2], 1)` µV, is close to it.

:::

---

## 2. Extracting information

### 2.1 How much do participants differ?

Use `VarCorr(m)` to find the SD of the participants' N400 effects. About 95% of participants should have an effect within two SDs of the fixed effect. Compute that range. Does every participant show an N400?

::: solution

```{r}
VarCorr(m)
slope_sd <- attr(VarCorr(m)$participant, "stddev")[2]
fixef(m)[2] + c(-2, 2) * slope_sd
```

Even at the edge of the range, the effect is negative: the model expects an N400 in practically every participant.

:::

### 2.2 Each participant's effect

`coef(m)$participant` gives each participant's own intercept and slope. Which participant has the weakest N400, and which the strongest?

::: solution

```{r}
by_participant <- coef(m)$participant |>
  rownames_to_column("participant")
by_participant |> slice_max(conditionunexpected)
by_participant |> slice_min(conditionunexpected)
```

:::

### 2.3 Confidence intervals

Compute 95% confidence intervals for the fixed effects with `confint(m, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")`. Report the N400 effect with its interval.

::: solution

```{r}
ci <- confint(m, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
ci
```

Unexpected words made the amplitude `r round(abs(fixef(m)[2]), 2)` µV more negative (95% CI [`r round(ci[2, 1], 2)`, `r round(ci[2, 2], 2)`]).

:::

### 2.4 Predictions

Predict the amplitude in each condition for an average participant and an average item, with `predict()` and `re.form = NA`.

::: solution

```{r}
new <- tibble(condition = c("expected", "unexpected"))
predict(m, newdata = new, re.form = NA)
```

These are the intercept and the intercept plus the slope.

:::

---

## 3. Significance testing

### 3.1 A likelihood ratio test

Fit `m` again with `REML = FALSE`, and a model without `condition` but with the same random effects, also with `REML = FALSE`. Compare them with `anova()`. Report χ², the degrees of freedom and p.

::: solution

```{r}
m_full <- lmer(amplitude ~ condition + (1 + condition | participant) + (1 | item),
               data = cz, REML = FALSE)
m_null <- lmer(amplitude ~ 1 + (1 + condition | participant) + (1 | item),
               data = cz, REML = FALSE)
lrt <- anova(m_null, m_full)
lrt
```

The model with the condition fits much better: χ²(`r lrt$Df[2]`) = `r round(lrt$Chisq[2], 1)`, p `r if (lrt[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2] < 0.001) "< .001" else paste("=", round(lrt[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], 3))`.

:::

### 3.2 p-values with `lmerTest`

Fit `m` again with `lmerTest::lmer()` and look at `summary()`. Find the degrees of freedom and the p-value of `conditionunexpected`.

::: {.solution .smaller}

```{r}
m_lt <- lmerTest::lmer(amplitude ~ condition + (1 + condition | participant) + (1 | item), data = cz)
summary(m_lt)$coefficients
```

The degrees of freedom are not a whole number: `lmerTest` approximates them, and they depend mostly on the number of participants and items, not on the `r nrow(cz)` trials. Both tests agree that the N400 effect is clearly different from 0.

:::

### 3.3 Bonus: cloze as a continuous predictor

The N400 depends on how predictable a word is, not only on the condition. Fit a model of `amplitude` as a function of `cloze`, with `(1 + cloze | participant) + (1 | item)`. What does the slope mean? Compare it with the true model in 1.3.

::: solution

```{r}
m_cloze <- lmer(amplitude ~ cloze + (1 + cloze | participant) + (1 | item), data = cz)
fixef(m_cloze)
```

From a word nobody expects (cloze 0) to a word everybody expects (cloze 1), the amplitude rises by `r round(fixef(m_cloze)[2], 1)` µV. In the true model this is 4 µV.

:::
